name: Preveli Monastery
seoTitle: Preveli Monastery, Crete: History Above the Palms
seoDescription: Preveli Monastery sits on a cliff above the Libyan Sea, 45 minutes from Rethymno, known for its WWII shelter of Allied soldiers and its view.
summary: The monastery of Preveli is the cliff-top building you see before you drop down to the palm beach: a working monastery with a view of the Libyan Sea, a small museum, and a real part in the story of the Battle of Crete. It is 45 minutes from Rethymno, free of the lagoon crowds, and the usual first stop on a south-coast day because the light on the courtyard is better in the morning.
body:
## The building

There are two monastic sites: Kato Preveli by the river, largely ruined, and Piso Preveli on the cliff, which is the one you visit. The present church and courtyard date from the nineteenth century rebuild after an Ottoman destruction. The view from the terrace is the one on the postcards — sea, gorge mouth, and the palm forest as a dark green smear below.

## The history

The monks sheltered Allied soldiers after the 1941 airborne invasion and helped get them off the island by submarine from the beach below. That is why British and Australian visitors still come, and why there is a memorial on the approach. The museum holds vestments, weapons and the usual Cretan monastic mix of liturgy and resistance.

## Practicalities

Admission is paid on site and is not included in the tour price; carry cash. Shoulders and knees covered. About 45 minutes from Rethymno via the Kourtaliotiko Gorge. Thirty to forty-five minutes is enough for the courtyard, the church and the view. The palm beach is a further descent — a separate stop, with its own parking and a walk or boat depending on how you do it. Closed on some religious days; check if you are self-driving at Easter.

faqs.q: Is Preveli Monastery the same as Preveli Beach?
faqs.a: No. The monastery sits on the cliff. The palm forest and lagoon are below, a separate stop with their own access. Most south-coast days from Rethymno do both.
It sheltered Allied soldiers after the Battle of Crete in 1941 and helped evacuate them from the beach below. It also stood in earlier Cretan resistance under Ottoman rule.
Yes, paid at the gate and not included in our tour price. Carry cash. The amount changes; it is a few euros.

faqs.q: How long do we spend there?
faqs.a: Half an hour to forty-five minutes is enough for the courtyard, the church, the small museum and the sea view. The beach is extra time.
